references.text: Isaiah prophesies about the Lord as a stone that people stumble over and a rock that causes the house of Israel to fall. Jesus alludes to this prophecy when he speaks of the stone that crushes whoever falls on it. See [ref:Jes 8:14-15|Isaiah 8:14-15].

In Daniel's vision of the statue, a stone is cut out without human hands and shatters the image into dust – the stone "crushes" whatever it falls on. This is the background for Jesus' words that the stone will "grind to powder" whoever it falls on. See [ref:Dan 2:34-35|Daniel 2:34-35].

Daniel's interpretation of the statue explains that the stone represents God's kingdom, which will crush all other kingdoms. Jesus uses the same image for himself as the decisive stone. See [ref:Dan 2:44-45|Daniel 2:44-45].

Isaiah speaks of a cornerstone, a precious foundation stone that God lays in Zion. Jesus identifies himself with this stone, which becomes either salvation or judgment depending on people's response. See [ref:Jes 28:16|Isaiah 28:16].
Matthew's parallel passage contains the same statement about the stone that crushes whoever falls on it and pulverizes whoever it falls on. See [ref:Matt 21:44|Matthew 21:44].

Peter quotes from the Psalms and Isaiah, describing Jesus as the cornerstone who becomes a stumbling block and a rock of offense to unbelievers – whoever falls over this stone will be destroyed. See [ref:1 Pet 2:7-8|1 Peter 2:7-8].

The psalm about the stone that builders rejected but which became the cornerstone is the direct context for Jesus' words in Luke 20:18. Jesus quoted this verse just before (Luke 20:17) and now expands on the consequences of rejecting this stone. See [ref:Sal 118:22|Psalm 118:22].

Paul quotes Isaiah and describes Christ as a stumbling block and a rock of offense in Zion – whoever believes in him will not be put to shame, but whoever stumbles over him will fall. See [ref:Rom 9:33|Romans 9:33].
